title: Past the veil
hookLine: the harper is told even his regret about the past is a veil to move beyond (Masnavi 1)

lines: THE SAME APOLOGY FOR TWENTY YEARS.
cards: Some people apologize for the same thing for twenty years. The friend who still brings up how she behaved at her sister's wedding. The dad who can't stop saying he worked too much when the kids were small.

The regret is real, and it was once useful. But at some point the regret itself becomes the thing they carry, heavier than whatever happened. The old harper is still on the grave, weeping over his whole life.
The caliph is about to say something surprising about those tears.

teach.h: EVEN YOUR TEARS ARE STILL ABOUT YOU.
teach.b: The harper is mourning his seventy years of music, the harp he just smashed, all the breath he spent on other people. You'd expect Umar to praise him: finally, real repentance.
Instead, in Rumi's telling, Umar says this weeping is also a sign that you're still awake to yourself. Your eyes are still on the past.
And the past and the future are veils between you and God. Burn them both. How long will you stay tied up in these knots?
A veil, in Rumi's language, is anything that hangs between you and what's real. Pride can be a veil. So can shame.
The harper had moved from one to the other: first proud of his voice, now sorry about it. Either way, the story is still about him. Umar invites him one step further, past both.
Rumi says the harper's heart woke up.
He stopped weeping, and he stopped laughing too. He went into a state Rumi says can't be described, and the poem simply lets him go. Sufis call this passing away of the small self fana.

The point doesn't depend on the word: there comes a time when even your regrets are just more ways of staring at yourself. Rumi isn't saying the past doesn't matter. He's saying you can't live facing backward.

And that brings the week together: the parrot that played dead to get free, Marcus's inner retreat, change as nature's favorite thing, and an old man who played for no one, was seen, and walked past the veil.

how: In Sufi teaching, repentance matters, but teachers often warn against getting stuck in regret; the goal described in stories like this is fana, a passing away of the self-centered self.

o: the passing away of the small self
losing all hope after a long grief

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: anything between you and what's real
still a way of looking at himself
the veils Umar tells him to burn
the passing away of the small self

s: Umar praises the harper's regret as the goal
he says even the weeping is a veil, still looking back at himself.
at the end, the harper stops laughing and weeping
Rumi says his heart woke and he went into a state beyond description.
Rumi says the past doesn't matter
the story doesn't erase the past. it says you can't live facing backward.

games.q: you're Umar. the old harper is sobbing over seventy wasted years. what do you say?
o: good, keep weeping; this is what repentance looks like.
your weeping is also a veil; move past the past and the future.
stop crying; the gold will fix everything.
games.why: Umar tells him his weeping is still a sign of being caught in himself, and that past and future are both veils.

practice: Find one thing you keep holding against yourself, something old, not something that still needs fixing, and look at it plainly for a breath or two.
Then imagine setting it down beside you, the way the harper finally put his weeping down. You're not pretending it didn't happen; you're just not carrying it for the next two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Fana. The Sufi term for the passing away of the small self, which Umar invites the weeping harper toward. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian, from Arabic: a veil or curtain. in Sufi writing, anything that hangs between a person and God.

carryVoice: Your line: burn them both. Even regret can become one more veil. That's the week.

sources.ref: Masnavi Book 1 (the old harper: Umar's words and the harper's passing beyond)
